descriptions.text: Compare the complete six-byte input needle with the literal needle. This measures a tiny equality check, not text scanning.
Check a six-byte prefix on a 32 KiB input. Only the leading needle is compared; the rest of the input is not scanned.

Check a six-byte suffix on a 32 KiB input. Only the final needle is compared. The historical benchmark ID says LARGE because the input is large, not because the suffix is long. This does not measure long-suffix performance.

Synthetic stress test: search 32 KiB of repeated aabx for aab followed by bba. The first literal matches immediately, but the second is absent despite many partial candidates. This deliberately unfavorable input is not representative of ordinary text; it measures rejection cost under dense false candidates.
Search 32 KiB of mostly x bytes for needle, either absent or near the end. Both cases require searching almost the complete input.
Find alpha followed by omega near the end of a 32 KiB input of mostly x bytes. The literal order matters; the intervening text is unrestricted.
Search 32 KiB for alpha, exactly one Unicode character, and omega. The matching input uses a four-byte emoji for the one-character gap; the other input has no match.
Search a 1 KiB input for alpha, bravo, and charlie separated by exactly one character each. The matching sequence is near the end.
Search text for dates and times using a large expression covering many formats, month names and time zones. This is much broader than checking one ISO date.
Find Python noqa comments and capture their optional lint-rule codes. The original form also captures preceding whitespace; the tweaked form removes that part.

Tokenize Veryl source code with one large alternation for keywords, identifiers, numbers, comments and punctuation. Capture groups identify which token alternative matched. The single suffix means one combined regex, not single-use compilation.
Parse semicolon-separated records from the Unicode character database and capture the fields on each line. This is structured-file parsing, not a scan of every possible Unicode character.
Scan source files for AWS credential-like strings. The quick pattern finds access-key IDs; the full pattern also looks for nearby secret-key-shaped text and captures the components.
Look for sequences of 10 to 100 capitalized words, allowing whitespace between them.
Find the word Result with ten-letter words nearby on both sides, allowing up to 100 intervening characters on each side. The input is Rust source code.
Find runs of 8 to 13 letters in English or Russian text. The Russian case uses a Unicode letter class.
Parse structured log lines into captured fields such as timestamp, severity, message and trailing metadata. Despite the benchmark name, the timed operation counts captures; it does not build JSON.
Search text for any word from a large dictionary expressed as one alternation. The english-10 and english-15 suffixes select minimum word lengths, not dictionaries of ten or fifteen words.
Search each source-code line for a complete ASCII word of at least 25 characters, and count the lines containing one.
Look for thirteen comma-terminated pieces followed immediately by z. The pieces can themselves contain commas, so there can be many possible ways to divide the text.
Look for Holmes followed by Watson, or vice versa, with up to ten repeated text-and-whitespace groups between them. These groups are not strict individual words and can overlap in many ways.
Find either ordering of two names or words within a bounded character distance. This searches for nearby occurrences, not just either word independently.
Find complete words ending in the specified n or nn suffix. Matching requires checking the word boundary as well as the suffix.
Repeatedly match as much text as dot permits. Line endings and zero-length matches still affect iteration; this is not simply returning the input length.
Match the whole document with dot-all enabled, then finish normal match iteration, including any terminal empty match. The benchmark sums matched lengths.
Search a book for an absent three-letter string. The variants change how common its individual letters are, which changes the amount of candidate checking even though none matches.
Search a manufactured input containing every Unicode scalar value. This tests Unicode handling across the full character range, not the distribution of characters in ordinary prose.
Try capturing 14 consecutive letters, then 13, and so on down to 5. This deliberately stresses overlapping alternatives, bounded repetition and capture recovery on English or Russian text.

Search English prose for whole words or word context. Some variants find all words or long words; around-holmes finds Holmes together with the word on either side. Word-character and boundary rules follow the selected regex language.
Find Bible references in prose and capture the book, chapters and verse ranges. The short case uses one small input; the long and line cases search a larger document.
Parse one tab-separated Caddy log record into timestamp, level, logger, message and optional extra fields.
Find Cargo registry paths and extract a package name and version. Variants use Unix separators, Windows separators, or support both.
Find URLs with a large expression covering hosts, IP addresses, paths and an explicit list of top-level domains. This is considerably more complex than checking for an http prefix.
Find programming-language keywords as complete words in real source code. This is an ordinary keyword-search workload that originally appeared in a performance bug report.

Find a starting character followed by a fixed-length run from an overlapping character class and a required ending character. Many partial matches can coexist, creating a difficult DFA state-growth case even on ordinary text.

Match exactly 256 word characters or Unicode letters against a constructed input of one repeated character. This probes the cost of large bounded repetitions, including the size of Unicode matching programs.
Reproduce a denial-of-service regex failure and simplified variants using repeated overlapping wildcards. The inputs are chosen to expose excessive retry work.

Try to match a long prefix ending in a non-capital letter, or fall back to one capital letter. On an all-capital input, repeated searches can revisit the same suffixes. The size variants expose this scaling behavior.
Use many repetitions of an overlapping A+ group, with an empty fallback, on a deliberately short all-A input. The variants increase pattern size as well as input size.
Try nested repetitions of a+ followed by a different letter against a short all-a input. This is a classic exponential-backtracking trap.

performance.text: This measures construction plus one match of the one-character wildcard with Trino's DFA optimization disabled. Neither engine builds a DFA here. Regulator constructs a literal-plus-gap plan; Trino uses its general LIKE parser and non-DFA matcher. Construction and first-call setup plausibly account for the small Intel disadvantage, rather than scanning a long input. The DFA-enabled row measures a different construction trade-off.

Both engines compare only six literal bytes. Regulator uses its shared Slice equality kernel, backed by Arrays.equals; Trino uses a small direct byte loop. Dispatch and equality-call setup are plausible contributors to Regulator's roughly 1-3 ns extra cost in these measurements. The percentage can look large because the entire operation takes only a few nanoseconds. This does not establish a disadvantage for longer literals.

Regulator recognizes these simple ASCII literal forms directly and builds a compact equality, prefix, or suffix plan. Trino uses its general LIKE parser. Cheaper construction can make Regulator faster for compilation plus first use even when the warmed six-byte comparison is slightly slower.

Regulator's shared literal scanner repeatedly finds positions with the right first and last bytes for bba but the wrong middle byte. After a bounded amount of failed comparison work, it switches to linear-time KMP scanning. Trino's FJS search combines skip tables with KMP and handles this repeated input more efficiently. Regulator takes about twice as long here. This is a real stress-case disadvantage, with linear scanning and bounded matching memory, not exponential backtracking. The scan dominates both single-use and multi-use timings.

Regulator reduces this pattern to Slice.indexOf instead of running a wildcard automaton. Trino uses its FJS literal search. Slice's accelerated byte search is a favorable fit for this mostly uniform input with an absent or late literal. The different search loops plausibly explain the large advantage; this is not a general ratio for arbitrary text.

Regulator uses the shared ordered-literal kernel, searching for each literal in sequence. Its scanner checks eight candidate positions at a time using the literal's first and last bytes, skipping this mostly x-filled input efficiently. Trino uses FJS searches for the same literals. Sparse candidates favor Regulator here; the dense-false stress case shows the opposite trade-off.

Regulator recognizes literals separated by fixed one-character gaps. The shared literal-plus-gap kernel searches for a literal, then checks the gap and following literals only at candidate positions. Trino routes these patterns through its NFA because an underscore follows a percent wildcard, even with DFA optimization enabled. Avoiding NFA processing across the input explains the large advantage on these sparse-candidate cases.

Trino has already built a DFA, so this one-character match needs only a few byte-table transitions. Regulator uses its literal-plus-gap matcher without DFA construction. Its per-call bookkeeping is a plausible source of the small execution disadvantage where Trino wins, usually less than 3 ns here. The winner depends on the CPU and character width.

This includes compilation and the first match. Trino constructs a dense DFA for the one-character pattern, costing tens of microseconds in these measurements. Regulator builds a compact literal-plus-gap plan in tens of nanoseconds. The very large speedup is a construction advantage, not a claim that each subsequent match is hundreds of times faster; the multi-use column measures that separately.
Regulator counts non-overlapping literal hits with the same accelerated prefix scanner used by boolean literal search, without running the DFA for each hit.
These short inputs use Regulator's shared byte-class scanner for contains and count, avoiding general-engine setup. Larger inputs keep the DFA's accelerated scanning path.
Contains currently uses the DFA even though finding one ASCII whitespace character is enough. A simpler scan may avoid some fixed overhead; the absolute difference here is small.

Count already uses a specialized character-run counter, but it handles general Unicode classes and decodes UTF-8. That is more machinery than this default Java ASCII-whitespace pattern needs, and is a plausible source of the small extra cost.

This measures counting every non-overlapping literal occurrence in the complete input, not just testing whether one exists. Match density and each engine's literal-search strategy affect the result; multilingual input alone does not explain the gap.

This lexer produces many tokens and requests captures identifying the chosen alternative. Regulator's capture bookkeeping remains expensive here; backtracking engines can record captures while following the successful token path. Tagged-capture handling reduces some of Regulator's cost but does not eliminate this disadvantage.

Regulator's extended one-pass capture support can handle larger capture-heavy programs than upstream RE2's compact one-pass representation. Avoiding a more general capture engine is a likely explanation for the large advantage on this combined lexer.

On a short matching input, capture handling and engine setup can dominate the actual scan. JDK Pattern and Joni record captures during backtracking; Regulator's selected capture path can carry more setup and bookkeeping. This is a likely fixed-cost disadvantage, not a measure of large-document throughput.

The JDK has tight loops for greedy character runs on its already-prepared UTF-16 input. Regulator must preserve UTF-8 character and match-iteration behavior. That difference appears relevant to this gap; dot-all removes newline restrictions but does not by itself make the full operation a constant-time length lookup.

These patterns combine word runs with boundaries, minimum lengths, context or suffix checks. Regulator's simple whole-word shortcut does not cover every such shape. More general matching work is a plausible contributor to the gap; support for a fast bare-word scan does not imply that this full expression uses it.

Regulator's specialized route scans word runs directly instead of resolving each simple word through the general matching machinery. This reduces per-word work, particularly when the input contains many short words.

A large literal alternation is a favorable case for compiled automata: many alternatives can share matching work. A backtracking engine may try many dictionary branches at candidate positions. This is the likely source of the large advantage, rather than faster character decoding.

This expression combines many alternatives with repeated URL components. Regulator can share work through its compiled automata and candidate-search shortcuts, while backtracking may revisit alternatives and positions. That is a plausible explanation for its advantage on this corpus.

The repeated pieces can divide the same text in many ways. Backtracking may revisit those combinations, especially when the required ending is absent. Regulator's automata avoid enumerating the same backtracking choices, which explains why these cases can show very large gaps or comparator timeouts.

Much of this document does not match. Regulator can use fast boundary searches to skip nonmatching text and do capture recovery only for matches. That balance is much more favorable than the short, capture-dominated version of the same pattern.

Regulator has a compact character-class run counter for eligible bounded repetitions. It can count runs without building or executing the large general automaton that repeated Unicode classes can otherwise require. This specialization is a likely contributor to the advantage here.

Regulator's specialized route searches for the required ending x first, then checks the fixed-length prefix backward. Sparse ending characters let it skip most of the corpus and avoid the DFA state-growth problem. Dense candidate endings can make this strategy less favorable.

The input is designed to make a backtracking engine revisit many choices before rejecting a match. Regulator uses finite-automaton algorithms rather than exploring those backtracking combinations. A comparator timeout here is a property of this stress case, not a general application speed ratio.
